Hi Samira — thanks for the example in the spreadsheet. I expanded with a small concrete mapping and a couple of gotchas.

1) Basic 3-turn example (human/system/human) — token accounting
- Prompt tokens: all input messages sent in the request (system + user + prior messages) are counted as input tokens.
- Completion tokens: the model output tokens are counted as output tokens.
- Example: System(25t) + User1(40t) + User2(30t) = 95 input tokens. Model reply = 120 output tokens. Billed = 95 input + 120 output.

2) Function call case — what to watch for
- If you use Responses with a function call, the function 'arguments' included in the model output count as output tokens. If you then serialize and send those arguments back as part of the next request, they become input tokens in the next call.
- So a typical flow: Model emits function args (60t) --> billed as 60 output tokens. You call your function, then include results (80t) in next input --> billed as 80 input tokens. No additional hidden fee, but double-counting across rounds is common if you mirror outputs back into inputs.

3) Streaming behavior
- For metering, tokens are accounted for the same whether delivered streaming or in a single chunk. Streaming does not create extra unit charges; only the final token counts matter. However, if you re-open the stream or request partials across multiple calls that replicate the same content, you'll incur additional input/output tokens accordingly.

4) Responses vs Chat parity
- Intent: parity on token units. In practice, Responses consolidates a few internal framing tokens and may be slightly more efficient on short system prompts. But for planning assume parity and add a 3-5% buffer for encoding/metadata differences.

5) Edge cases to budget for
- Long-running KV cache: if you rely on KV cache to avoid resending shared context, you'll lower input tokens (good). But cache misses during rollouts can spike costs.
- Function-heavy integrations (heavy JSON args) increase output tokens.
- Prompt templating that expands on every request (e.g., echoing full user history) will increase input tokens linearly.

I'll attach a short CSV with the example calculations. If you'd like, I can generate a scanned-sample invoice mapping for your finance team with the same example.

Hi Samira — attaching the hosted baseline rate card PDF and a brief FAQ for procurement. A few practical notes from billing: 

- Baseline hosted rates (excerpt attached):
  • Chat/Responses base: $0.0025 per 1k input tokens; $0.0060 per 1k output tokens (example model family rates).
  • Streaming does not change unit prices.
  • Function outputs are billed as output tokens. Any subsequent request that includes those outputs as input will be billed as input tokens.

- Discounts / committed terms: For deals with committed monthly spend (>= $25k/mo) we typically layer tiered discounts and offer a billing SOW with explicit token buckets. For NEO-2026-447 we can propose a draft commitment schedule once you confirm expected monthly token volumes.

- Invoicing IDs & reconciliation: please add the HubSpot deal ID (NEO-2026-447) to your PO and we'll ensure the invoice line items include model, endpoint type, and token breakdowns.
